name: Dolores "Lola" Reyes
text:
# The Spark
Quick, bright, and always starting something.
Cheerful by disposition. Restless by make-up.
Strongest leanings: Speaks up, Simply glad, Open-handed

## Your type
You bring energy. Your mood is light and you hate sitting still. You would rather try something and laugh about it later than wait and wonder. People catch your enthusiasm. A quiet week makes you restless, and a full one makes you happy.
Where the trap is set for you: pleasure. "For because pleasure borders on mirth, he holds out lust as a bait to cheerful dispositions." (St Gregory the Great, Moralia on Job) So your temptation rarely looks like temptation. It looks like a good time. One more drink, one more episode, one more look than you meant to give.
What you bring: You get things going. You make hard things feel lighter. You bounce back fast.
What it costs you: You start more than you finish. You can rush past what needed thought. Quiet feels like a threat, so you fill it.
Kindred: Augustine, as a young man: Before his conversion he loved talk, jokes, reading together and friendly arguments. He was just as honest, later, about where his love of pleasure had led him.
Your opposite: The Deep Well (Thoughtful, grave, and feels things all the way down.)

## Your leanings
- Mood: Light-hearted <-> Heavy-hearted: Light-hearted (21/100)
- Nerve: Confident <-> Careful: balanced (42/100)
- Make-up: Restless mind <-> Quiet mind: Restless mind (0/100)
- Talk: Speaks up <-> Keeps it in: Speaks up (8/100)
- Candour: Says it plainly <-> Chooses what to show: Says it plainly (25/100)
- When wronged: Lets them know <-> Lets it go: Lets it go (83/100)
- Temper: Fiery <-> Gentle: balanced (58/100)
- Disagreements: Takes a stand <-> Keeps the peace: Keeps the peace (83/100)
- Pace: Rushes in <-> Puts it off: Rushes in (25/100)
- Follow-through: Hard to start <-> Hard to finish: balanced (58/100)
- Little things: Careful with little things <-> Easy on little things: balanced (42/100)
- Your own work: Sure of your work <-> Hard on yourself: balanced (58/100)
- Correction: Say it straight <-> A hint is enough: A hint is enough (83/100)
- Room: Takes up room <-> Makes yourself small: Takes up room (17/100)
- Your mind: Holds firm <-> Easily swayed: Holds firm (25/100)
- Others' wins: Simply glad <-> Feels the sting: Simply glad (8/100)
- Seen and unseen: Better in public <-> Better in private: Better in public (33/100)
- After a mistake: Dwells on a mistake <-> Moves on: Dwells on a mistake (33/100)
- Having: Open-handed <-> Careful with what you have: Open-handed (8/100)
- Comforts: Enjoys comforts <-> Keeps a tight rein: Enjoys comforts (25/100)
Most like you: Speaks up, Simply glad, Open-handed. Balanced: Your own work, Little things, Follow-through
* Speaks up: You think out loud, and you are easy to talk to. What you may not see: Much talk scatters the mind, Gregory says, so it loses touch with itself. And idle talk slides, step by step, into talk about other people. "it has no power to turn back within to the knowledge of itself" (St Gregory the Great, Moralia on Job) Counsel: Before you speak, ask whether it is needed, or kind.
* Simply glad: You are glad when others do well. What you may not see: Admiring is not the same as trying. Gregory warns about cheering from the stands. "eager backers, but inert spectators" (St Gregory the Great, Pastoral Rule) Counsel: If you admire it, try it.
* Open-handed: You give easily. What you may not see: Gregory warns the generous against giving so much at once that they run short and start grumbling. "when the soul of the giver knows not how to endure want, then, in withdrawing much from himself, he seeks out against himself occasion of impatience" (St Gregory the Great, Pastoral Rule) Counsel: Give steadily and cheerfully, and do not keep score.

## What you might not have noticed
- You said you let rudeness go. You also said hours later you think of what you should have said. You win in the moment by staying calm. Then, on a quiet evening, it comes back bigger than it was. You can end up wishing you had been harsher than you would ever actually be. The hard part for you is not staying calm. It is the evening after. "blushes for having borne such things calmly, and is sorry that he did not return insults" (St Gregory the Great, Pastoral Rule)
- You said you let things slide that you probably should not. You also said you calm things down when friends argue. Gregory says gentleness has a next-door neighbour, and it is letting things go that should not go. Keeping the peace can be love. It can also be the easier road. "Sloth is frequently looked upon as a maintenance of peace" (St Gregory the Great, Moralia on Job)
- You said you are nothing but glad when friends succeed. You also said you admire lots of people you never try to be like. That gladness is rare and good. Gregory’s one warning is for people exactly like you: do not only cheer from the stands. Admire it enough to try it. "eager backers, but inert spectators" (St Gregory the Great, Pastoral Rule)
- You said a mistake stays with you for a long time. You also said you say sorry a lot, and sometimes do it again anyway. Gregory describes people who wash, and then walk straight back into the mud. Feeling bad is real, but it cannot do the work of changing. The sorrow is meant to lead somewhere. 

## How your anger works
Slow and brief. It takes a lot to anger you, and it does not last. Gregory says this is the one closest to peace of mind.  One caution from Chrysostom: calm that is never tested is not yet patience. Stay among people.

## How you speak
Fluent, not deep. Words come easily, sometimes before the thought is ready. Of the four kinds of speaker, Gregory blames only this one, and says it needs holding back. The fix is simple: think first.

## How to help me
1. Ask for my help. I will give it gladly.
2. Give me room to think out loud.
3. Show me. Let me see someone do it.
4. Slow me down. I run ahead.
5. Tell me what I did well. It makes me try harder.
6. Tell me in private.
7. Do not push. I come round in my own time.

## Where the fight is for you now (private)
Right now: Gluttony. Not eating well. Reaching for food or drink to take the edge off, or wanting something nicer than what is in front of you. Gregory says the fault is never in the food. It is in the wanting. How it talks to you: "God has created all things clean, in order to be eaten" (Gregory, Moralia on Job, gluttony’s own speech) How it shows: Eating when you are not hungry. Wanting the dish to be different. A heavy, dull mind afterwards. What feeds it: It comes first on Cassian’s list, and it opens the door to the others. What takes its place: Cassian’s advice is steady, daily moderation, not sudden strict fasts. And break your own fast gladly for a guest.
All eight: Gluttony 100, Sadness 83, Vainglory 73, Pride 67, Greed 48, Listlessness 42, Anger 36, Lust 12. Troubles you least: Lust.

## Your best quality, and its counterfeit
Diligence: You keep working when others stop. Counterfeit: Restlessness. Not being able to stop can feel like faithfulness. "Restlessness of spirit is frequently termed a watchful solicitude" (St Gregory the Great, Moralia on Job)
Your strength: Courage. Its partner: Counsel. You act bravely. The risk is acting before you have thought it through.

## Who you are in Christ, and in the Body
Your gladness is a gift. Kept close to God, it becomes the joy Christ promised, the kind nobody can take from you. "I will see you again, and your heart shall rejoice, and your joy no man shall take from you" (Christ, quoted by Gregory in the Pastoral Rule)
Your line: The Host (hospitality). You serve by opening your door. A meal, a bed, a welcome. People feel at home with you. Cassian names Abraham and Lot, and in his own day Macarius, who ran a guest house in Alexandria and was known as "a man of singular courtesy and patience". Second: The Caregiver.
(They picked: gladly do: Have them round and cook for them. / Sit with them while they’re ill or struggling.; people come for: A welcome, and somewhere to be. / Practical help, or a loan.)

Zeal: You care about right and wrong, and you act on it. Counterfeit: Temper that calls itself zeal. Anger can borrow the clothes of righteousness. "unbridled wrath is accounted the virtue of spiritual zeal" (St Gregory the Great, Pastoral Rule)

text:
# The Still Water
Listens first, keeps the peace, and thinks it through.
Careful by disposition. Quiet by make-up.
Strongest leanings: Puts it off, Hard to start, Careful with what you have

## Your type
You take things in before you let anything out. You would rather listen than talk, and you would rather keep the peace than win. A crowded week wears you down faster than it does most people. Give you quiet and you do your best thinking. People trust you, because you are careful with them.
Where the trap is set for you: fear. "Because the timid dread punishments, he threatens terrors to the fearful." (St Gregory the Great, Moralia on Job) So your temptation rarely looks like temptation. It looks like worry. What if they are upset? What if it goes wrong? What if I say it, and it costs me?
What you bring: You listen, and people can tell. You are slow to judge out loud. You rarely make an enemy.
What it costs you: You say less than you mean. You carry hurts home with you. You wait to be sure, and sometimes the moment passes.
Kindred: St Gregory the Theologian: He loved "calm and retirement" from his youth, and ran away when they made him a priest. When his best friend Basil called him lazy, he wrote back: "My greatest business always is to keep free from business." Near the end he said, "I am weary of being charged with my gentleness." | Jeremiah: When God called him, he pleaded that he was too young to speak. Gregory says he held back out of love: he longed to stay close to God in quiet. | Abba Arsenius: A desert monk who fled the world to pray. In an old story he is seen sailing in silence, with the Spirit of God beside him.
Your opposite: The Herald (Steps forward, speaks up, and gets things moving.)
Close call: your second disposition is close; you could also be The Deep Well.

- Nerve: Confident <-> Careful: Careful (79/100)

Most like you: Puts it off, Hard to start, Careful with what you have. Balanced: Your own work, Temper, Disagreements
* Puts it off: You wait until you are sure. What you may not see: The slow, Gregory says, find something reasonable to be afraid of, and call it a reason to wait. "The sluggard would not plough by reason of the cold" (Proverbs, as Gregory quotes it for the slow) Counsel: Start before you feel ready.
* Hard to start: The first step is the hardest part. What you may not see: Gregory says people who never begin are usually busy with something else they love. That has to be seen for what it is first.  Counsel: Name what is holding you back. Then take one step.
* Careful with what you have: You keep a little back. What you may not see: Holding on can call itself thrift. Gregory adds that grasping often grows from fear of running short. "Tenacity is sometimes considered frugality" (St Gregory the Great, Moralia on Job) Counsel: Give something away this week that you might have kept.

## What you might not have noticed
- You said more of your regrets are things you never got round to. You also said before something big you think about what could go wrong. Those are one habit. You picture the setbacks, and the picture keeps you still. Gregory quotes Proverbs about a farmer who would not plough because it was cold, and then had nothing to harvest. "The sluggard would not plough by reason of the cold" (Proverbs, as Gregory quotes it)
- You said your gut says “let me think” when a friend asks for money. You also said you worry about having enough, even when you have plenty. Gregory says grasping grows from two roots, pride and fear, and yours looks like fear. It is not greed for more. It is fear of less. That is worth knowing, because fear is answered differently from greed. "avarice sometimes steals upon men from pride, and sometimes from apprehension" (St Gregory the Great, Moralia on Job)
- You said you listen more than you talk. You also said you have whole conversations in your head that never happen. Those are the same thing. The talking does not stop. It moves inside, where nobody can answer back. And an argument nobody can answer is easy to win. It can leave you quietly judging people who never got to reply. "For his tongue he represses, his mind he exalts" (St Gregory the Great, Pastoral Rule)
- You said you let rudeness go. You also said hours later you think of what you should have said. You win in the moment by staying calm. Then, on a quiet evening, it comes back bigger than it was. You can end up wishing you had been harsher than you would ever actually be. The hard part for you is not staying calm. It is the evening after. "blushes for having borne such things calmly, and is sorry that he did not return insults" (St Gregory the Great, Pastoral Rule)

## How your anger works
Hard wood. It takes a lot to make you angry. But once it is lit, it stays lit. It just burns where no one can see it. "others, like the heavier and harder kinds of wood, are slow in taking fire, but being once kindled, are with difficulty put out" (St Gregory the Great, Moralia on Job) Gregory’s cure for your kind is to see it coming. Before the day starts, think through what might go wrong and how you will meet it calmly. A blow you expected lands softer.

## How you speak
Deep, but held in. You think deeply, but the words come hard. Gregory knew this speaker and did not blame them. He said they need help getting it out. Try writing it down first, or saying it to one person instead of a room.

## How to help me
1. Explain why. I need the reasons.
2. Give me a push. I am slow to get going.
3. Ask what I think. I rarely offer it.
4. Tell me in private.
5. Argue it out with me. Win fairly and I will come round.
6. Tell me plainly what you need.
7. Say it straight. I can take it.

## Where the fight is for you now (private)
Right now: Greed. Not always wanting more. Often it is fear of having less. Cassian says it starts with "excellent and almost reasonable excuses". How it talks to you: "It is a very blameless thing, that thou desirest some things to possess; because thou seekest not to be increased, but art afraid of being in want" (Gregory, Moralia on Job, greed’s own speech) How it shows: Keeping a reserve "just in case". Worrying about old age and illness. It is never quite enough. What feeds it: Gregory says sadness runs down into it: a heart with no joy inside looks for comfort in owning things. What takes its place: Cassian says cut the desire, not only the spending. Be content with what you need.
All eight: Greed 100, Listlessness 91, Sadness 65, Pride 59, Gluttony 30, Anger 29, Lust 18, Vainglory 12. Troubles you least: Vainglory.

## Your best quality, and its counterfeit
Deliberation: You think before you move. Counterfeit: Delay. Putting off can pass for thinking it through. "tardiness for the deliberation of seriousness" (St Gregory the Great, Pastoral Rule)
Your strength: Counsel. Its partner: Courage. You think it through well. The risk is that you never get round to doing it.

## Who you are in Christ, and in the Body
Your care is a gift. Gregory says the fearful should not stay in fear but grow, fed by love, until love does what fear used to do. "grow up by the nursing of charity to the grace of love" (St Gregory the Great, Pastoral Rule)
Your line: The Giver (giving). You serve by giving. Money, time, things. You notice what people need and you meet it. Cassian names people who "give alms to the poor" among the lines God gives. Second: The Teacher.
(They picked: gladly do: Give them something they need. / Explain something that helps them understand.; people come for: Practical help, or a loan. / Advice, or something explained.)

# The Herald
Steps forward, speaks up, and gets things moving.
Confident by disposition. Restless by make-up.
Strongest leanings: Takes up room, Speaks up, Hard to finish

## Your type
When something needs doing, you volunteer. You are sure of yourself and you like to be moving. People follow you because you go first. You would rather try and fail than never try.
Where the trap is set for you: praise. "And because he beholds the proud elated with praises, he draws them on to whatever he pleases, by flattering applause." (St Gregory the Great, Moralia on Job) So your temptation rarely looks like temptation. It looks like applause. Whoever praises you can steer you.
What you bring: Courage to go first. You get people moving. You say what others are afraid to.
What it costs you: You can promise more than you can keep. Praise can steer you. You do not always check who is following.
Kindred: Isaiah: When God asked, "Whom shall I send?", he did not wait to be asked twice: "Here am I. Send me!" | St Peter: "Even if all fall away on account of You, I never will," he said, the night before he denied Christ three times. Then he wept, came back, and led the Church. | St Basil the Great, as a young man: His brother says Basil came home from university proud of his speaking and looking down on the local grandees, until his sister Macrina turned him round.
Your opposite: The Still Water (Listens first, keeps the peace, and thinks it through.)

Most like you: Takes up room, Speaks up, Hard to finish. Balanced: Candour, Comforts, Seen and unseen
* Takes up room: You speak up to people in charge. What you may not see: Some of it may be pride that thinks it is honesty. "so do some speak from the impatience of pride, and yet think that they are speaking with rightful freedom" (St Gregory the Great, Moralia on Job) Counsel: Before you speak up, check what is driving it.

* Hard to finish: You start well, then fade. What you may not see: Gregory says a soul is like a boat going upstream. Stop rowing and it does not stay put. It drifts back. "in the condition of a ship ascending against the stream of a river" (St Gregory the Great, Pastoral Rule) Counsel: Finish one thing before you start the next.

2. Give me room to think out loud.
3. Challenge me. I can handle it.
4. Slow me down. I run ahead.
5. Be specific about what could be better.
6. Show me. Let me see someone do it.
7. Tell me what I did well. It makes me try harder.

Frankness: You say what needs saying. Counterfeit: Pride. Pride can feel like simple honesty. "so do some speak from the impatience of pride, and yet think that they are speaking with rightful freedom" (St Gregory the Great, Moralia on Job)
Your strength: Courage. Its partner: Counsel. You act bravely. The risk is acting before you have thought it through.

Your confidence is not a flaw to be crushed. Bowed before God, it becomes the courage to speak up for what is right. "Some are lifted up by pride. # The Deep Well
Thoughtful, grave, and feels things all the way down.
Serious by disposition. Quiet by make-up.
Strongest leanings: Heavy-hearted, Fiery, Takes a stand

## Your type
You feel things deeply and think them through. You are serious by nature, and you need quiet to be at your best. People come to you when something really matters, because you will not treat it lightly. You notice what others miss, including what is wrong.
Where the trap is set for you: a quarrel. "And because moroseness easily slides into anger, he offers the cup of discord for the morose." (St Gregory the Great, Moralia on Job) So your temptation rarely looks like temptation. It looks like being right about how badly you have been treated.
What you bring: Depth. You take people seriously. You are honest about sorrow. You notice what others miss.
What it costs you: Heaviness can become your home. Hurts go deep and stay there. Joy can feel suspicious.
Kindred: St Gregory the Great: The man whose book this quiz is built on. He opens his Dialogues alone in a place he says suited "a sad and melancholy disposition", and he wrote that he loved the quiet life and had the busy one forced on him. | Elijah: After his great victory on Carmel he ran into the wilderness and sat under a tree. "I have had enough, LORD," he said. The desert fathers remembered him as the one who "loved silence".
Your opposite: The Spark (Quick, bright, and always starting something.)

## Your leanings

* Fiery: You feel the heat, and you act on it. What you may not see: The hot-tempered, Gregory says, mistake their anger for righteousness. (St Gregory the Great, Moralia on Job)
- You said you listen more than you talk. You also said you have whole conversations in your head that never happen. Those are the same thing. The talking does not stop. It moves inside, where nobody can answer back. And an argument nobody can answer is easy to win. It can leave you quietly judging people who never got to reply. "For his tongue he represses, his mind he exalts" (St Gregory the Great, Pastoral Rule)
- You said you tell people in charge when they are wrong. You also said your anger usually feels justified. Gregory would call that a pair. 1. Do not push. I come round in my own time.
2. Say "next time, try this", not "you did this wrong".
3. Show me. Let me see someone do it.
4. Ask for my help. I will give it gladly.
5. Ask what I think. I rarely offer it.
6. Say it straight. I can take it.
7. Give me a push. I am slow to get going.

# The Still Water
Listens first, keeps the peace, and thinks it through.
Careful by disposition. Quiet by make-up.
Strongest leanings: Lets it go, Keeps the peace, Puts it off

## Your type
You take things in before you let anything out. You would rather listen than talk, and you would rather keep the peace than win. A crowded week wears you down faster than it does most people. Give you quiet and you do your best thinking. People trust you, because you are careful with them.
Where the trap is set for you: fear. "Because the timid dread punishments, he threatens terrors to the fearful." (St Gregory the Great, Moralia on Job) So your temptation rarely looks like temptation. It looks like worry. What if they are upset? What if it goes wrong? What if I say it, and it costs me?
What you bring: You listen, and people can tell. You are slow to judge out loud. You rarely make an enemy.
What it costs you: You say less than you mean. You carry hurts home with you. You wait to be sure, and sometimes the moment passes.
Kindred: St Gregory the Theologian: He loved "calm and retirement" from his youth, and ran away when they made him a priest. When his best friend Basil called him lazy, he wrote back: "My greatest business always is to keep free from business." Near the end he said, "I am weary of being charged with my gentleness." | Jeremiah: When God called him, he pleaded that he was too young to speak. Gregory says he held back out of love: he longed to stay close to God in quiet. | Abba Arsenius: A desert monk who fled the world to pray. In an old story he is seen sailing in silence, with the Spirit of God beside him.
Your opposite: The Herald (Steps forward, speaks up, and gets things moving.)

* Lets it go: You stay calm when you are wronged. What you may not see: The patient often feel nothing at the time. Later they remember it, and start looking for ways to get even. "when after a while they recall to memory these very same things that they have endured, they inflame themselves with the fire of vexation" (St Gregory the Great, Pastoral Rule) Counsel: Guard your heart after the win. * Keeps the peace: You calm things down. What you may not see: Gregory warns the peaceable not to love peace so much that they never tell anyone they are wrong. You can end up wishing you had been harsher than you would ever actually be. The hard part for you is not staying calm. It is the evening after. Slow and brief. It takes a lot to anger you, and it does not last. Gregory says this is the one closest to peace of mind.  One caution from Chrysostom: calm that is never tested is not yet patience. Stay among people.

Full in both. You think things through, and the words come easily. Gregory calls this speaker "worthy of praise". The gift is meant to be used for others.

3. Tell me what I did well. It makes me try harder.
4. Tell me in private.

Right now: Listlessness. The desert fathers called it the noonday demon. A weariness of heart that makes where you are feel unbearable and anywhere else look better. Its argument is pious. What takes its place: Cassian says its place is taken by courage. His remedy is plain: work with your hands, and stay put.
All eight: Listlessness 100, Gluttony 47, Greed 47, Vainglory 38, Lust 26, Sadness 26, Anger 19, Pride 12. Troubles you least: Pride.

Peace: You calm things. People are safer around you. Counterfeit: Avoidance. Staying out of trouble can pass for keeping the peace. "Sloth is frequently looked upon as a maintenance of peace" (St Gregory the Great, Moralia on Job)
Your strength: Counsel. Its partner: Courage. You think it through well. The risk is that you never get round to doing it.

Your care is a gift. Gregory says the fearful should not stay in fear but grow, fed by love, until love does what fear used to do. "grow up by the nursing of charity to the grace of love" (St Gregory the Great, Pastoral Rule)
Your line: The Host (hospitality). You serve by opening your door. A meal, a bed, a welcome. People feel at home with you. Cassian names Abraham and Lot, and in his own day Macarius, who ran a guest house in Alexandria and was known as "a man of singular courtesy and patience". Second: The Caregiver.

Quick, bright, and always starting something.

Alert, conscientious, and sees the risks first.

## Your type
You are the one who thinks ahead. You keep busy, and you keep an eye on what could go wrong. People trust you with things that matter, because you will not be careless with them. You would rather over-prepare than be caught out.
Where the trap is set for you: fear. "Because the timid dread punishments, he threatens terrors to the fearful." (St Gregory the Great, Moralia on Job) So your temptation rarely looks like temptation. It looks like worry. What if they are upset? What if it goes wrong? What if I say it, and it costs me?
What you bring: Foresight. Faithfulness in the details. People can rely on you.
What it costs you: Worry keeps you busy. You can mistake fear for wisdom. You say yes to too much, afraid of letting people down.
Kindred: Moses: When God called him he said, "I am slow of speech and tongue," and begged God to send someone else. Then he led a whole people through the desert for forty years. | Gideon: "My clan is the weakest in Manasseh, and I am the youngest in my father’s house," he said. He obeyed God, but he did it at night, because he was afraid.
Your opposite: The Oak (Self-possessed, steady, and needs no one’s approval.)

Warm, steady, and glad to be where you are.
Cheerful by disposition. Quiet by make-up.
Strongest leanings: Hard to finish, Careful with what you have, Enjoys comforts

## Your type
You are easy to be around. Your mood is light, and you do not need to be busy to be happy. People relax when you walk in. You enjoy things as they come: a meal, a long talk, an evening at home. You do not go looking for trouble, and it rarely finds you.
Where the trap is set for you: pleasure. "For because pleasure borders on mirth, he holds out lust as a bait to cheerful dispositions." (St Gregory the Great, Moralia on Job) So your temptation rarely looks like temptation. It looks like a good time. One more drink, one more episode, one more look than you meant to give.
What you bring: People feel welcome around you. You enjoy the good things you are given. You do not make things harder than they are.
What it costs you: You can settle for comfortable. You would rather not look at what is wrong. Pleasure can quietly become the point.
Kindred: St Antony the Great: He spent twenty years alone in the desert. When he came out, Athanasius says, his friends were amazed at how settled he was, and his face was cheerful because his soul was at peace.

* Hard to finish: You start well, then fade. What you may not see: Gregory says a soul is like a boat going upstream. Stop rowing and it does not stay put. It drifts back. * Careful with what you have: You keep a little back. What you may not see: Holding on can call itself thrift. Gregory adds that grasping often grows from fear of running short. - You said your mood is usually light. You also said after a hard day you treat yourself. A light heart is a gift. - You said more of your regrets are things you never got round to. You also said before something big you think about what could go wrong. Those are one habit. Your gladness is a gift. Kept close to God, it becomes the joy Christ promised, the kind nobody can take from you. "I will see you again, and your heart shall rejoice, and your joy no man shall take from you" (Christ, quoted by Gregory in the Pastoral Rule)

# The Still Water
Listens first, keeps the peace, and thinks it through.
Careful by disposition. Quiet by make-up.
Strongest leanings: Keeps it in, Puts it off, Careful with what you have

You take things in before you let anything out. You would rather listen than talk, and you would rather keep the peace than win. A crowded week wears you down faster than it does most people. Give you quiet and you do your best thinking. People trust you, because you are careful with them.
Where the trap is set for you: fear. "Because the timid dread punishments, he threatens terrors to the fearful." When his best friend Basil called him lazy, he wrote back: "My greatest business always is to keep free from business." Near the end he said, "I am weary of being charged with my gentleness." | Jeremiah: When God called him, he pleaded that he was too young to speak. Gregory says he held back out of love: he longed to stay close to God in quiet. | Abba Arsenius: A desert monk who fled the world to pray. Hard wood. It takes a lot to make you angry. But once it is lit, it stays lit. It just burns where no one can see it. Full in both. You think things through, and the words come easily. Gregory calls this speaker "worthy of praise". The gift is meant to be used for others.

1. Explain why. I need the reasons.
2. Give me a push. I am slow to get going.

Right now: Listlessness. The desert fathers called it the noonday demon. A weariness of heart that makes where you are feel unbearable and anywhere else look better. Its argument is pious. What takes its place: Cassian says its place is taken by courage. His remedy is plain: work with your hands, and stay put.

## Your best quality, and its counterfeit
Deliberation: You think before you move. Counterfeit: Delay. Putting off can pass for thinking it through. "tardiness for the deliberation of seriousness" (St Gregory the Great, Pastoral Rule)
Your strength: Counsel. Its partner: Courage. You think it through well. The risk is that you never get round to doing it.

## Who you are in Christ, and in the Body
Your care is a gift. Gregory says the fearful should not stay in fear but grow, fed by love, until love does what fear used to do. "grow up by the nursing of charity to the grace of love" (St Gregory the Great, Pastoral Rule)
Your line: The Teacher (teaching). You serve by helping people understand. You explain, you make it clear, you pass it on. Cassian names people who "give themselves up to teaching" as one of the lines God gives. Second: The Giver.

"it has no power to turn back within to the knowledge of itself" (St Gregory the Great, Moralia on Job) Counsel: Before you speak, ask whether it is needed, or kind.
* Chooses what to show: You are careful what people see of you. What you may not see: Keeping up a guard is tiring work. Gregory says the plain truth is the safest thing there is. "there is nothing safer for defense than sincerity, nothing easier to say than truth" (St Gregory the Great, Pastoral Rule) Counsel: Let one person see all of you.

## What you might not have noticed
- You said a mistake stays with you for a long time. You also said you say sorry a lot, and sometimes do it again anyway. Gregory describes people who wash, and then walk straight back into the mud. Feeling bad is real, but it cannot do the work of changing. The sorrow is meant to lead somewhere. 
- You said you keep your disagreements with people in charge to yourself. You also said you never think your work is good enough. Those grow from one root. Some of what feels like humility may be fear of how it will land. Only you can tell which is which, but it is worth asking. "just as many are silent through fear, and yet consider that they are silent from humility" (St Gregory the Great, Moralia on Job)
- You said your mood is usually light. You also said after a hard day you treat yourself. A light heart is a gift. Gregory adds one warning: pleasure lives right next door to cheerfulness, so it is the one pull you are least guarded against. "For because pleasure borders on mirth, he holds out lust as a bait to cheerful dispositions." (St Gregory the Great, Moralia on Job)
- You said a friend’s success stings a little. You also said you notice quickly when someone is doing better than you. Gregory says we only envy people we think are better than us in some way. So the sting is a compliment you have not said out loud. Say it, and the sting weakens. "Those things, in fact, are ours which we love in others" (St Gregory the Great, Pastoral Rule)

## How your anger works
Slow and brief. It takes a lot to anger you, and it does not last. Gregory says this is the one closest to peace of mind.  One caution from Chrysostom: calm that is never tested is not yet patience. Stay among people.

## How you speak
Fluent, not deep. Words come easily, sometimes before the thought is ready. Of the four kinds of speaker, Gregory blames only this one, and says it needs holding back. The fix is simple: think first.

## How to help me
1. Slow me down. I run ahead.
2. Tell me in private.
3. Ask for my help. I will give it gladly.
4. Give me room to think out loud.
5. Explain why. I need the reasons.
6. Tell me what I did well. It makes me try harder.
7. Hold me to the details. I let things slip.

## Where the fight is for you now (private)
Right now: Listlessness. The desert fathers called it the noonday demon. A weariness of heart that makes where you are feel unbearable and anywhere else look better. Its argument is pious. Cassian says it suggests good reasons to leave, like a visit that would be "a real work of piety". How it shows: Watching the clock. Drifting from task to task. Suddenly wanting to visit someone, go somewhere, do anything but the thing in front of you. What feeds it: Cassian says sadness feeds it. What takes its place: Cassian says its place is taken by courage. His remedy is plain: work with your hands, and stay put.

## Your best quality, and its counterfeit
Diligence: You keep working when others stop. Counterfeit: Restlessness. Not being able to stop can feel like faithfulness. "Restlessness of spirit is frequently termed a watchful solicitude" (St Gregory the Great, Moralia on Job)
Your strength: Courage. Its partner: Counsel. You act bravely. The risk is acting before you have thought it through.

## Who you are in Christ, and in the Body
Your gladness is a gift. Kept close to God, it becomes the joy Christ promised, the kind nobody can take from you. "I will see you again, and your heart shall rejoice, and your joy no man shall take from you" (Christ, quoted by Gregory in the Pastoral Rule)
Your line: The Teacher (teaching). You serve by helping people understand. You explain, you make it clear, you pass it on. Cassian names people who "give themselves up to teaching" as one of the lines God gives. Second: The Shepherd.

# The Forge
Intense, driven, and cannot stand things done badly.
Serious by disposition. Restless by make-up.
Strongest leanings: Lets it go, Makes yourself small, Careful with what you have

## Your type
You care hard and you move fast. You are serious about what matters, and you cannot rest while it is wrong. People know where they stand with you. You get done what others only talk about.
Where the trap is set for you: a quarrel. "And because moroseness easily slides into anger, he offers the cup of discord for the morose." (St Gregory the Great, Moralia on Job) So your temptation rarely looks like temptation. It looks like being right about how badly you have been treated.
What you bring: Conviction. You fix what others only complain about. You tell the truth when it is needed.
What it costs you: Your anger feels like justice, even when it is not. You wear people out, yourself included. Rest feels like losing.
Kindred: St John Chrysostom: A friend from his youth called him irritable, and an admiring historian says it was his nature to rebuke wrongdoing. He preached so hard against the powerful that he died in exile. | St Jerome: The great translator of the Bible was a fighter by his own account. He wrote that in an argument he threw himself into the thick of it.
Your opposite: The Hearth (Warm, steady, and glad to be where you are.)
Close call: your second disposition is close; you could also be The Lookout.

## Your leanings
- Mood: Light-hearted <-> Heavy-hearted: Heavy-hearted (79/100)
- Nerve: Confident <-> Careful: Careful (75/100)
- Make-up: Restless mind <-> Quiet mind: Restless mind (38/100)
- Talk: Speaks up <-> Keeps it in: Keeps it in (67/100)
- Candour: Says it plainly <-> Chooses what to show: Chooses what to show (75/100)
- When wronged: Lets them know <-> Lets it go: Lets it go (92/100)
- Temper: Fiery <-> Gentle: balanced (58/100)
- Disagreements: Takes a stand <-> Keeps the peace: balanced (50/100)
- Pace: Rushes in <-> Puts it off: balanced (50/100)
- Follow-through: Hard to start <-> Hard to finish: Hard to start (33/100)
- Little things: Careful with little things <-> Easy on little things: Careful with little things (17/100)
- Your own work: Sure of your work <-> Hard on yourself: balanced (50/100)
- Correction: Say it straight <-> A hint is enough: balanced (58/100)
- Room: Takes up room <-> Makes yourself small: Makes yourself small (92/100)
- Your mind: Holds firm <-> Easily swayed: Holds firm (25/100)
- Others' wins: Simply glad <-> Feels the sting: Feels the sting (67/100)
- Seen and unseen: Better in public <-> Better in private: balanced (50/100)
- After a mistake: Dwells on a mistake <-> Moves on: Dwells on a mistake (25/100)
- Having: Open-handed <-> Careful with what you have: Careful with what you have (92/100)
- Comforts: Enjoys comforts <-> Keeps a tight rein: Keeps a tight rein (92/100)
Most like you: Lets it go, Makes yourself small, Careful with what you have. Balanced: Seen and unseen, Your own work, Pace
* Lets it go: You stay calm when you are wronged. What you may not see: The patient often feel nothing at the time. Later they remember it, and start looking for ways to get even. "when after a while they recall to memory these very same things that they have endured, they inflame themselves with the fire of vexation" (St Gregory the Great, Pastoral Rule) Counsel: Guard your heart after the win. Say the hurt calmly, and soon.
* Makes yourself small: You keep to the edge until you are sure. What you may not see: Some of it may be fear that thinks it is humility. "just as many are silent through fear, and yet consider that they are silent from humility" (St Gregory the Great, Moralia on Job) Counsel: Humility does not mean silence. Say the true thing, kindly.
* Careful with what you have: You keep a little back. What you may not see: Holding on can call itself thrift. Gregory adds that grasping often grows from fear of running short. "Tenacity is sometimes considered frugality" (St Gregory the Great, Moralia on Job) Counsel: Give something away this week that you might have kept.

## What you might not have noticed
- You said you let rudeness go. You also said hours later you think of what you should have said. You win in the moment by staying calm. Then, on a quiet evening, it comes back bigger than it was. You can end up wishing you had been harsher than you would ever actually be. The hard part for you is not staying calm. It is the evening after. "blushes for having borne such things calmly, and is sorry that he did not return insults" (St Gregory the Great, Pastoral Rule)
- You said you hold back after a hard day. You also said you notice when other people overindulge. Gregory says self-denial has its own temptation, and it is not food. It is looking down on people who do not go without. Discipline is a gift. Judging the undisciplined is where it turns. "the pride of abstinence" (St Gregory the Great, Moralia on Job)
- You said things stay with you for a while. You also said once you are angry, it can last for days. Gregory saw the link. A heavy heart slides easily into anger, and a slow anger turns into a grudge. They feed each other. "And because moroseness easily slides into anger, he offers the cup of discord for the morose." (St Gregory the Great, Moralia on Job)
- You said your gut says “let me think” when a friend asks for money. You also said you worry about having enough, even when you have plenty. Gregory says grasping grows from two roots, pride and fear, and yours looks like fear. It is not greed for more. It is fear of less. That is worth knowing, because fear is answered differently from greed. "avarice sometimes steals upon men from pride, and sometimes from apprehension" (St Gregory the Great, Moralia on Job)

## How your anger works
Hard wood. It takes a lot to make you angry. But once it is lit, it stays lit. It just burns where no one can see it. "others, like the heavier and harder kinds of wood, are slow in taking fire, but being once kindled, are with difficulty put out" (St Gregory the Great, Moralia on Job) Gregory’s cure for your kind is to see it coming. Before the day starts, think through what might go wrong and how you will meet it calmly. A blow you expected lands softer.

## How you speak
Deep, but held in. You think deeply, but the words come hard. Gregory knew this speaker and did not blame them. He said they need help getting it out. Try writing it down first, or saying it to one person instead of a room.

## How to help me
1. Show me. Let me see someone do it.
2. Tell me in private.
3. Do not push. I come round in my own time.
4. Say "next time, try this", not "you did this wrong".
5. Slow me down. I run ahead.
6. Tell me what I did well. It makes me try harder.
7. Let some things go. Too much correction and I give up.

## Where the fight is for you now (private)
Right now: Greed. Not always wanting more. Often it is fear of having less. Cassian says it starts with "excellent and almost reasonable excuses". How it talks to you: "It is a very blameless thing, that thou desirest some things to possess; because thou seekest not to be increased, but art afraid of being in want" (Gregory, Moralia on Job, greed’s own speech) How it shows: Keeping a reserve "just in case". Worrying about old age and illness. It is never quite enough. What feeds it: Gregory says sadness runs down into it: a heart with no joy inside looks for comfort in owning things. What takes its place: Cassian says cut the desire, not only the spending. Be content with what you need.
All eight: Greed 100, Listlessness 78, Anger 76, Sadness 69, Vainglory 43, Pride 35, Gluttony 31, Lust 12. Troubles you least: Lust.

## Your best quality, and its counterfeit
Humility: You do not need to be the centre. Counterfeit: Fear. Keeping quiet out of fear can feel like humility. "just as many are silent through fear, and yet consider that they are silent from humility" (St Gregory the Great, Moralia on Job)
Your strength: Counsel. Its partner: Courage. You think it through well. The risk is that you never get round to doing it.

## Who you are in Christ, and in the Body
Your seriousness is not a flaw to be fixed. Held under reason, the fire in it becomes holy zeal. "For some are possessed by anger, but while they submit this to reason, they convert it into service rendered to holy zeal." (St Gregory the Great, Moralia on Job)
Your line: The Caregiver (caring for the sick and struggling). You serve by staying close when things are hard. You sit with people, and you do not leave. Cassian names people who "choose the care of the sick" among the lines God gives. Second: The Watcher.
(They picked: gladly do: Sit with them while they’re ill or struggling. / Pray for them quietly, and keep on praying.; people come for: Care when things are hard. / Practical help, or a loan.)

# The Herald
Steps forward, speaks up, and gets things moving.
Confident by disposition. Restless by make-up.
Strongest leanings: Takes a stand, Takes up room, Speaks up

## Your type
When something needs doing, you volunteer. You are sure of yourself and you like to be moving. People follow you because you go first. You would rather try and fail than never try.
Where the trap is set for you: praise. "And because he beholds the proud elated with praises, he draws them on to whatever he pleases, by flattering applause." (St Gregory the Great, Moralia on Job) So your temptation rarely looks like temptation. It looks like applause. Whoever praises you can steer you.
What you bring: Courage to go first. You get people moving. You say what others are afraid to.
What it costs you: You can promise more than you can keep. Praise can steer you. You do not always check who is following.
Kindred: Isaiah: When God asked, "Whom shall I send?", he did not wait to be asked twice: "Here am I. Send me!" | St Peter: "Even if all fall away on account of You, I never will," he said, the night before he denied Christ three times. Then he wept, came back, and led the Church. | St Basil the Great, as a young man: His brother says Basil came home from university proud of his speaking and looking down on the local grandees, until his sister Macrina turned him round.
Your opposite: The Still Water (Listens first, keeps the peace, and thinks it through.)
Close call: your second disposition is close; you could also be The Spark.

## Your leanings
- Mood: Light-hearted <-> Heavy-hearted: Light-hearted (21/100)
- Nerve: Confident <-> Careful: Confident (17/100)
- Make-up: Restless mind <-> Quiet mind: Restless mind (38/100)
- Talk: Speaks up <-> Keeps it in: Speaks up (8/100)
- Candour: Says it plainly <-> Chooses what to show: balanced (42/100)
- When wronged: Lets them know <-> Lets it go: Lets them know (25/100)
- Temper: Fiery <-> Gentle: Fiery (8/100)
- Disagreements: Takes a stand <-> Keeps the peace: Takes a stand (0/100)
- Pace: Rushes in <-> Puts it off: balanced (50/100)
- Follow-through: Hard to start <-> Hard to finish: balanced (42/100)
- Little things: Careful with little things <-> Easy on little things: Careful with little things (8/100)
- Your own work: Sure of your work <-> Hard on yourself: Sure of your work (17/100)
- Correction: Say it straight <-> A hint is enough: Say it straight (25/100)
- Room: Takes up room <-> Makes yourself small: Takes up room (0/100)
- Your mind: Holds firm <-> Easily swayed: Holds firm (33/100)
- Others' wins: Simply glad <-> Feels the sting: Simply glad (25/100)
- Seen and unseen: Better in public <-> Better in private: balanced (50/100)
- After a mistake: Dwells on a mistake <-> Moves on: Moves on (83/100)
- Having: Open-handed <-> Careful with what you have: balanced (50/100)
- Comforts: Enjoys comforts <-> Keeps a tight rein: Keeps a tight rein (67/100)
Most like you: Takes a stand, Takes up room, Speaks up. Balanced: Having, Seen and unseen, Pace
* Takes a stand: You say where you stand. What you may not see: Gregory says many quarrels grow from pride in a gift that sets us apart, like knowing more or trying harder.  Counsel: Win the point without losing the person.
* Takes up room: You speak up to people in charge. What you may not see: Some of it may be pride that thinks it is honesty. "so do some speak from the impatience of pride, and yet think that they are speaking with rightful freedom" (St Gregory the Great, Moralia on Job) Counsel: Before you speak up, check what is driving it.
* Speaks up: You think out loud, and you are easy to talk to. What you may not see: Much talk scatters the mind, Gregory says, so it loses touch with itself. And idle talk slides, step by step, into talk about other people. "it has no power to turn back within to the knowledge of itself" (St Gregory the Great, Moralia on Job) Counsel: Before you speak, ask whether it is needed, or kind.

## What you might not have noticed
- You said you tell people in charge when they are wrong. You also said your anger usually feels justified. Gregory would call that a pair. What feels like honesty can be pride, and what feels like zeal can be temper. Neither means you are wrong. It means the feeling of being right is not proof. "they think the goad of their anger to be the zeal of righteousness" (St Gregory the Great, Pastoral Rule)
- You said you fix things and move on. You also said you stop doing the wrong thing, but rarely say sorry. Stopping is good. But Gregory says it does not undo what was done, any more than a debtor clears a debt by borrowing no more. Something still needs saying. "nor is a debtor absolved by not increasing his debt, unless he also pays what he has incurred" (St Gregory the Great, Pastoral Rule)
- You said you are careful about small things. You also said your worst mistakes are rare, but big. Gregory knew this pattern well. Being careful in small things can make us feel safe, and the feeling of safety is where the big fall comes from. "Straining out a gnat, but swallowing a camel" (Christ, as Gregory quotes Him)
- You said you let people know on the spot. You also said you snap, and wish you had not. Gregory saw this exactly. Anger drives you somewhere you never meant to go, and you only see it when it is over. It is not that you do not care. It is that the care arrives too late. "fury drives the mind whither desire draws it not" (St Gregory the Great, Pastoral Rule)

## How your anger works
Slow and brief. It takes a lot to anger you, and it does not last. Gregory says this is the one closest to peace of mind.  One caution from Chrysostom: calm that is never tested is not yet patience. Stay among people.

## How you speak
Full in both. You think things through, and the words come easily. Gregory calls this speaker "worthy of praise". The gift is meant to be used for others.

## How to help me
1. Ask for my help. I will give it gladly.
2. Give me room to think out loud.
3. Explain why. I need the reasons.
4. Tell me what I did well. It makes me try harder.
5. Argue it out with me. Win fairly and I will come round.
6. Be specific about what could be better.
7. Challenge me. I can handle it.

## Where the fight is for you now (private)
Right now: Pride. Last on Cassian’s list, and first in its roots. Every other fault spoils one virtue. Pride spoils them all.  How it shows: Finding correction hard to take, even when it is fair. Thinking every serious talk is aimed at you. What feeds it: Cassian says vainglory feeds it. What takes its place: Cassian says its place is taken by humility, built on kindness and a simple heart.
All eight: Pride 100, Anger 74, Gluttony 71, Vainglory 71, Sadness 36, Listlessness 31, Lust 18, Greed 12. Troubles you least: Greed.

## Your best quality, and its counterfeit
Frankness: You say what needs saying. Counterfeit: Pride. Pride can feel like simple honesty. "so do some speak from the impatience of pride, and yet think that they are speaking with rightful freedom" (St Gregory the Great, Moralia on Job)
Your strength: Courage. Its partner: Counsel. You act bravely. The risk is acting before you have thought it through.

## Who you are in Christ, and in the Body
Your confidence is not a flaw to be crushed. Bowed before God, it becomes the courage to speak up for what is right. "Some are lifted up by pride. But whilst they bow down the mind to the fear of God, they change this into the free tone of unrestrained authority in defence of justice." (St Gregory the Great, Moralia on Job)
Your line: The Teacher (teaching). You serve by helping people understand. You explain, you make it clear, you pass it on. Cassian names people who "give themselves up to teaching" as one of the lines God gives. Second: The Giver.
(They picked: gladly do: Explain something that helps them understand. / Give them something they need.; people come for: Advice, or something explained. / Practical help, or a loan.)

# The Hearth
Warm, steady, and glad to be where you are.
Cheerful by disposition. Quiet by make-up.
Strongest leanings: Says it plainly, Puts it off, Hard to start

## Your type
You are easy to be around. Your mood is light, and you do not need to be busy to be happy. People relax when you walk in. You enjoy things as they come: a meal, a long talk, an evening at home. You do not go looking for trouble, and it rarely finds you.
Where the trap is set for you: pleasure. "For because pleasure borders on mirth, he holds out lust as a bait to cheerful dispositions." (St Gregory the Great, Moralia on Job) So your temptation rarely looks like temptation. It looks like a good time. One more drink, one more episode, one more look than you meant to give.
What you bring: People feel welcome around you. You enjoy the good things you are given. You do not make things harder than they are.
What it costs you: You can settle for comfortable. You would rather not look at what is wrong. Pleasure can quietly become the point.
Kindred: St Antony the Great: He spent twenty years alone in the desert. When he came out, Athanasius says, his friends were amazed at how settled he was, and his face was cheerful because his soul was at peace.
Your opposite: The Forge (Intense, driven, and cannot stand things done badly.)

## Your leanings
- Mood: Light-hearted <-> Heavy-hearted: Light-hearted (29/100)
- Nerve: Confident <-> Careful: balanced (54/100)
- Make-up: Restless mind <-> Quiet mind: Quiet mind (67/100)

- Correction: Say it straight <-> A hint is enough: Say it straight (25/100)
- Room: Takes up room <-> Makes yourself small: balanced (42/100)
- Your mind: Holds firm <-> Easily swayed: Holds firm (33/100)
- Others' wins: Simply glad <-> Feels the sting: Simply glad (33/100)
- Seen and unseen: Better in public <-> Better in private: Better in private (67/100)
- After a mistake: Dwells on a mistake <-> Moves on: Moves on (75/100)
- Having: Open-handed <-> Careful with what you have: Careful with what you have (75/100)
- Comforts: Enjoys comforts <-> Keeps a tight rein: Enjoys comforts (17/100)
Most like you: Says it plainly, Puts it off, Hard to start. Balanced: Temper, Room, Little things
* Says it plainly: You say what you think. What you may not see: Gregory tells the plain-spoken that truth at the wrong moment can hurt people. They must learn when to keep quiet about what is true. "to know how sometimes to be silent about what is true" (St Gregory the Great, Pastoral Rule) Counsel: Keep your honesty. Choose your moment.
* Puts it off: You wait until you are sure. What you may not see: The slow, Gregory says, find something reasonable to be afraid of, and call it a reason to wait. "The sluggard would not plough by reason of the cold" (Proverbs, as Gregory quotes it for the slow) Counsel: Start before you feel ready.
* Hard to start: The first step is the hardest part. What you may not see: Gregory says people who never begin are usually busy with something else they love. That has to be seen for what it is first.  Counsel: Name what is holding you back. Then take one step.

## What you might not have noticed
- You said you let people know on the spot. You also said you snap, and wish you had not. Gregory saw this exactly. Anger drives you somewhere you never meant to go, and you only see it when it is over. It is not that you do not care. It is that the care arrives too late. "fury drives the mind whither desire draws it not" (St Gregory the Great, Pastoral Rule)
- You said you fix things and move on. You also said you stop doing the wrong thing, but rarely say sorry. Stopping is good. But Gregory says it does not undo what was done, any more than a debtor clears a debt by borrowing no more. Something still needs saying. "nor is a debtor absolved by not increasing his debt, unless he also pays what he has incurred" (St Gregory the Great, Pastoral Rule)
- You said your mood is usually light. You also said after a hard day you treat yourself. A light heart is a gift. Gregory adds one warning: pleasure lives right next door to cheerfulness, so it is the one pull you are least guarded against. "For because pleasure borders on mirth, he holds out lust as a bait to cheerful dispositions." (St Gregory the Great, Moralia on Job)
- You said you are nothing but glad when friends succeed. You also said you admire lots of people you never try to be like. That gladness is rare and good. Gregory’s one warning is for people exactly like you: do not only cheer from the stands. Admire it enough to try it. "eager backers, but inert spectators" (St Gregory the Great, Pastoral Rule)

## How your anger works
Kindled reeds. Your anger flares and is gone. You rarely hold a grudge. The danger is the first minute: what you say before it burns out. "like kindled reeds, while they clamour with their voices, give out something like a crackle at their kindling" (St Gregory the Great, Moralia on Job) Gregory’s cure for you: when someone wrongs you, remember your own faults first. It takes the heat out.

## How you speak
Fluent, not deep. Words come easily, sometimes before the thought is ready. Of the four kinds of speaker, Gregory blames only this one, and says it needs holding back. The fix is simple: think first.

## How to help me
1. Give me a push. I am slow to get going.
2. Tell me plainly what you need.
3. Say it straight. I can take it.
4. Be specific about what could be better.
5. Explain why. I need the reasons.
6. Tell me what I did well. It makes me try harder.
7. Hold me to the details. I let things slip.

## Where the fight is for you now (private)
Right now: Gluttony. Not eating well. Reaching for food or drink to take the edge off, or wanting something nicer than what is in front of you. Gregory says the fault is never in the food. It is in the wanting. How it talks to you: "God has created all things clean, in order to be eaten" (Gregory, Moralia on Job, gluttony’s own speech) How it shows: Eating when you are not hungry. Wanting the dish to be different. A heavy, dull mind afterwards. What feeds it: It comes first on Cassian’s list, and it opens the door to the others. What takes its place: Cassian’s advice is steady, daily moderation, not sudden strict fasts. And break your own fast gladly for a guest.
All eight: Gluttony 100, Pride 87, Listlessness 56, Anger 53, Sadness 51, Vainglory 27, Greed 26, Lust 12. Troubles you least: Lust.

## Your best quality, and its counterfeit
Deliberation: You think before you move. Counterfeit: Delay. Putting off can pass for thinking it through. "tardiness for the deliberation of seriousness" (St Gregory the Great, Pastoral Rule)
Your strength: Counsel. Its partner: Courage. You think it through well. The risk is that you never get round to doing it.

## Who you are in Christ, and in the Body
Your gladness is a gift. Kept close to God, it becomes the joy Christ promised, the kind nobody can take from you. "I will see you again, and your heart shall rejoice, and your joy no man shall take from you" (Christ, quoted by Gregory in the Pastoral Rule)
Your line: The Teacher (teaching). You serve by helping people understand. You explain, you make it clear, you pass it on. Cassian names people who "give themselves up to teaching" as one of the lines God gives. Second: The Host.
